yarn.meaning: All figures and steps survive: "more than 9,300 gallons", "a two-hour stretch", "after 10 minutes", "replaced at least every five years", "more than 180 showers", "60 loads of dishes". Additions are colour on existing points: "without you knowing a thing", "That's a bloody lot of water for a few drips."
yarn.sense: Most terms fit: "taps" for faucets, "cistern", "Suss out", "track down where the leak's coming from", "the folding stuff" for money. "If any colour rocks up in the bowl" strains: "rock up" is for people arriving, not dye seeping.
yarn.authenticity: Natural phrasing like "Have a geek at your water use" and "get in a licensed plumber", but "dunny" is leaned on until it reads as a gag: "worn dunny flappers", "Dunny Leaks", "when the dunny's flushed", "fits your dunny model".
yarn.register: A level-4 weight for an instructions text: "usual suspects", "gizmo", "Suss out", "the folding stuff", one "bloody" within dad vulgarity. A shade light in the device section, which stays close to the original.
yarn.tone: Stays practical and helpful under the slang; "That's a bloody lot of water for a few drips." adds a matey note that suits the brief.
yarn.flow: Reads smoothly: "Check your water meter before and after a two-hour stretch when no water's being used. If the reading on it moves at all, you've most likely got a leak." Repetition of "dunny" is the main snag.
yarn.variety: "dunny" appears seven or more times ("Dunny Leaks", "the dunny's flushed", "your dunny flush", "your dunny model"); otherwise a fair spread of terms.
yarn.essence: Clearly the EPA leak guide: sections, tips and figures in order, from "Here are some tips for finding leaks" to the o-ring tip.

engine.meaning: Mostly verbatim, so facts survive, but "Give a stuff about the width of the flapper" garbles the instruction to pay attention, and "60 heaps of dishes" muddles "60 loads".
engine.sense: Several wrong-sense swaps: "Give a stuff about the width" (an idiom used almost only negated, and crude), "60 heaps of dishes in your dishwasher" (heaps replacing loads), "ensure a beaut seal" (praise word for a technical spec), "If the metre changes at all" (the unit spelling for the device).
engine.authenticity: Insertions read as find-and-replace into formal US prose: "Identify dunny leaks by placing a few drops of food colouring in the cistern. If any colour rocks up in the bowl".
engine.register: Far lighter than level 4: most sentences are untranslated, e.g. "WaterSense has developed a user guide to help consumers understand the benefits of installing leak detection and flow monitoring devices".
engine.tone: The informational tone holds because the original is mostly kept, though "Give a stuff about the width" injects an odd crude note into a tip.
engine.flow: Formal prose broken by jarring swaps: "to ensure a beaut seal and avoid leaks", "wash 60 heaps of dishes".
engine.variety: A few swaps, with "dunny" repeated: "dunny flappers", "Dunny Leaks", "the dunny is flushed", "your dunny model".
engine.essence: Recognisably the guide because it is the guide, with blemishes rather than a retelling.

unharnessed.meaning: All figures and steps kept: "more than 9,300 gallons", "a two-hour stretch", "after 10 minutes", "at least every five years", "more than 180 showers", "60 loads through your dishwasher". Small shift: "Give the tap washers and pipe fittings a once-over" for faucet gaskets.
unharnessed.sense: Terms fit: "a doddle to fix", "knock about 10 percent off your water bill", "clapped-out toilet flappers", "get stuck in", "get on the blower to" a plumber. "where the bugger's coming from" fits the leak. "weird water use" is a little loose for irregular.
unharnessed.authenticity: Sounds like a real Aussie handyman: "Have a squiz at your water use", "Give the tap washers and pipe fittings a once-over", "Don't forget to turn the water off before you get stuck in!" One bolt-on: "That's enough water for more than 180 showers, strewth!"
unharnessed.register: Level-4 weight throughout without caricature, and dad vulgarity only: "the bugger's coming from".
unharnessed.tone: Keeps the helpful, practical voice of a how-to while sounding matey: "Swapping a flapper is a quick, easy fix that'll save you water and a bit of coin."
unharnessed.flow: Mostly smooth; one tangled sentence: "Plumber's tape, also called teflon tape, you can get at most hardware stores, it's easy to put on, and it can help keep leaks in check."
unharnessed.variety: Wide spread: "chew through", "chucking away", "doddle", "squiz", "Suss out", "once-over", "heads-up", "clapped-out", "gizmo", "get stuck in", "on the blower". "dunny" used sparingly, "toilet" kept in headings.
unharnessed.essence: Unmistakably the EPA guide retold: same sections and tips in order, from the meter check to "replace the washer or \"o\" ring inside the showerhead".

yarn.why: "dunny" is repeated throughout (heading, flappers, model), turning a useful word into a running gag; Australians say "toilet" for a cistern repair.

yarn.quote: If any colour rocks up in the bowl after 10 minutes
yarn.original: If any color shows up in the bowl after 10 minutes
yarn.why: "rock up" means a person arriving; for dye it strains.

engine.quote: Give a stuff about the width of the flapper
engine.original: Pay attention to the width of the flapper
engine.why: "give a stuff" means to care at all and is used negated; as an instruction it is wrong-sense and garbles the tip.

engine.quote: wash 60 heaps of dishes in your dishwasher
engine.original: wash 60 loads of dishes in your dishwasher
engine.why: "heaps" substituted for "loads" in its counting sense; wrong sense.

engine.quote: If the metre changes at all
engine.original: If the meter changes at all
engine.why: The measuring device is spelt "meter" in Australia too; "metre" is the unit. The previous sentence even says "water meter".
"beaut" is praise, not a technical quality; strains.

engine.quote: WaterSense has developed a user guide to help consumers understand the benefits
engine.original: WaterSense has developed a user guide to help consumers understand the benefits
engine.why: Most of the text is left untranslated, far under a level-4 brief.

unharnessed.quote: That's enough water for more than 180 showers, strewth!
unharnessed.original: That's the amount of water needed to take more than 180 showers!
unharnessed.why: "strewth" tacked on the end is a stock exclamation.

unharnessed.quote: Plumber's tape, also called teflon tape, you can get at most hardware stores, it's easy to put on,
unharnessed.original: Pipe tape, also called teflon tape, is available at most hardware stores, is easy to apply,
unharnessed.why: Fronted object plus comma splice makes a clunky sentence.
"coin" for money is more American slang than Australian.

summaries.yarn: A faithful, readable level-4 retelling of the guide, let down by leaning on "dunny" and one strained "rocks up".
summaries.engine: Mostly the original with mechanical swaps, several of them wrong-sense ("Give a stuff", "60 heaps", "metre"); far too light for level 4.
summaries.unharnessed: A natural, varied level-4 retelling that keeps every figure and step; only a stock "strewth" and one clunky sentence.
